inherit.why: true for this child because the dumbbells are still held in a closed grip and pressed overhead; the palm turn changes the hand's direction, not the thumb wrap. Parent c2 (ACE: thumbs wrapped around the handles) holds; ACE's line is carried here as c15 (MECH).

true for this child because each wrist still sits under a dumbbell pressed straight up; parent c2 and c6 (ACE: neutral wrists pressing and lowering) hold at every point of the turn. Carried here as c15 (MECH).
true for this child because it is the same seated dumbbell press over the head; ACE's spotter behind, hands near the wrists (c10 here, from the parent's source) is written for that position.
true for this child because the back-on-pad rule is the same and this card's own source names back arching as the fault (c3).

claims.text: Start with the dumbbells in front of the chest, palms facing you; turn the palms out as you press so they face forward at the top; turn them back in as you lower.

quotes.text: Start with the dumbbells in front of your chest with your palms facing toward your body.
As you press the dumbbells up, rotate your palms outward so they face forward when your arms are extended overhead.
Lower the dumbbells back to the starting position, rotating your palms inward again.

claims.text: Sit on a bench set upright (vertical, or just short of it).

quotes.text: Grab a bench and ensure that it is placed on the maximum incline position.
Sit on a bench, with either a slight decline from 90 degrees or completely vertical.

claims.text: Do not lift the back away from the bench during the press.

quotes.text: DON’T raise your back away from the bench during the lift.

claims.text: At the bottom the palms face you with the upper arms level with the floor; keeping them there through the turn keeps the shoulders loaded.

quotes.text: At the lowest point, your upper arms should be parallel to the floor and your palms facing you.
The most important part of the exercise is to keep your upper arms parallel to the ground at the lowest point and throughout the twist.
This keeps the tension on your deltoids all the way through.

claims.text: Getting in: rest the dumbbells on the knees, then kick them up to the pressing position.

quotes.text: Hold the dumbbells on your knees to start, then kick them up into a normal shoulder press position

claims.text: Go slightly lighter than on a normal dumbbell shoulder press.

quotes.text: We recommend you go slightly lighter in weight than with a normal shoulder press.

claims.text: Stop, or switch exercise, at any pain.

quotes.text: If you begin to experience any pain at all, you should stop the workout or switch to another exercise.

claims.text: The Arnold press mainly works the front and side of the shoulder (coach sources; no EMG study of the Arnold press was found).

quotes.text: The Arnold Press is a variation of the dumbbell shoulder press that primarily targets the front and medial parts of the shoulder.
The Arnold Press works your whole shoulder muscle, with emphasis on the front deltoid coming from the twist at the lowest point.

claims.text: Triceps activity was measured in barbell and dumbbell shoulder presses and differed between them (about 39% higher standing with a barbell than with dumbbells); the abstract gives no size for triceps work on its own, so for the Arnold press this is inferred from the dumbbell press and weakly supported.

quotes.text: Electromyogram activity was measured in the anterior, medial, and posterior deltoids and biceps and triceps brachii.
For triceps, ~39% greater for standing barbell versus dumbbells (p < 0.001), ~20% lower for seated versus standing barbell (p = 0.094).

claims.text: A way out on seated dumbbell presses: the spotter stands behind, hands close to the wrists without touching (written for the seated dumbbell press, the parent).

quotes.text: The spotter should stand behind you in a split-stance position, positioning their hands close to your wrists (not touching) to support you as needed.

claims.text: Add load in small steps: ACSM recommends a 2-10% increase once the current load can be done for one to two reps over the target.

quotes.text: it is recommended that 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number

claims.text: ACSM recommends a moderate speed for strength work: 1-2 seconds up and 1-2 seconds down.

quotes.text: using 3- to 5-min rest periods between sets performed at a moderate contraction velocity (1-2 s CON; 1-2 s ECC)

claims.text: Up to 36% of documented resistance-training injuries are at the shoulder, and poor attention to technique is a named risk factor.

quotes.text: The results of the review indicated that up to 36% of documented RT-related injuries and disorders occur at the shoulder complex.
extrinsic risk factors, namely, that of improper attention to exercise technique

claims.text: Across US emergency-department weight-training injuries, the most common mechanism was weights dropping on the person, and 90% involved free weights.

quotes.text: The most common mechanism of injury was weights dropping on the person (65.5%). A large number of injuries occurred with free weights (90.4%).

claims.text: On the seated dumbbell press (the parent), ACE uses a closed grip with the thumbs wrapped round the handles and keeps the wrists neutral, not bent forward or back, while pressing and lowering; inferred for the Arnold press, whose grip turns during the rep.

quotes.text: slowly lift the dumbbells to your shoulder level with a closed, pronated grip (palms facing forward and thumbs wrapped around the handles), with the dumbbells at shoulder-width or slightly wider and wrists in a neutral position (avoid flexion and extension of the wrists).
Maintain your body contact with the bench, neutral wrist (avoid flexion and extension) and depressed, retracted scapulae positions.

claims.text: Squeeze the grip as tight as you can as you press.

quotes.text: Breathing out and squeezing the grip as tight as you can, press the dumbbells up overhead, bringing them slightly in front of your head.

plate.viewWhy: Census view is side. The palm turn is a forearm roll the engine cannot draw, so the plate shows what reads from the side: back on the upright pad, dumbbells in front of the chest at the start, arms straight overhead at the end (c1, c3). The turn is covered in text and a hand close-up.
plate.equipment: Upright bench with a backrest, vertical or just short of it (c2); a dumbbell in each hand.
plate.start: Seated, back on the pad (c3); dumbbells in front of the chest, palms facing you (c1), upper arms about level with the floor (c4).
plate.end: Arms straight overhead, palms facing forward (c1), back still on the pad (c3).

checkpoints.label: Back on pad
checkpoints.what: The back stays against the bench for the whole press.

checkpoints.label: Palms in
checkpoints.what: At the bottom the dumbbells sit in front of the chest, palms toward you.

checkpoints.label: Arms straight up
checkpoints.what: At the top the arms are extended overhead, palms forward.

mistake.what: Back arching away from the pad as the dumbbells go up.
mistake.why: The Gym Group names it as the one thing not to do; the parent's top fault is the same. How often it happens is not measured in any source read.

tells.text: Palms face you at the bottom

grip.type: Closed grip that turns during the rep: palms toward you at the bottom, forward at the top (c1).
grip.width: Dumbbells in front of the chest at the bottom (c1); pressed to straight arms overhead.
grip.handContact: Handle squeezed tight in the hand (c16).
grip.wrist: Neutral, not bent forward or back, through the turn (inherited, parent c2, c6; c15).

setup.step: Sit with the dumbbells on your knees, then kick them up.
Dumbbells in front of your chest, palms facing you.
If using a spotter, they stand behind you, hands near your wrists.

posture.point: Palms face you at the bottom, forward at the top.
Upper arms about level with the floor at the bottom.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Arching the back off the bench.
handlingMistakes.fix: Keep your back on the pad.
Go a little lighter than your shoulder press.
Stop, or switch to another exercise.

rows.where: Front and sides of the shoulders
Pain in the shoulder during the turn or the press
rows.fix: Stop the set, or switch exercise.

risks.risk: Shoulder injuries are common in lifting and linked to poor technique.
Weights dropping on the lifter is the most common weight-room injury mechanism.
Adding weight in big jumps. Add 2-10% only once you can do one or two reps over your target.

zooms.right: Palms toward you at the bottom, turning to face forward as you press.
zooms.wrong: Palms already forward at the bottom (no turn: a normal shoulder press).
Back arched away from the pad.

libraryDiff.why: exercises.json: front_delts and side_delts primary; triceps secondary. c8 supports both deltoids (StrengthLog lists the lateral deltoid as secondary, Fit Father says the whole shoulder); no EMG study of the Arnold press was found, so no change on coach opinion alone. Triceps rests on c9 (MECH, WEAK).
